cultivar: Nanchuan Dashu, a local tree-form landrace of the Jinfo Mountain area
processing: Made as a green tea in two grades: the top grade from a single bud up to one bud with one open leaf, the standard grade from one bud with two leaves or three just opening. The detailed steps are not published beyond the national green tea standards it has to meet.
harvest_season: The picking standards are set by grade rather than by date; as with other Chongqing mountain greens, spring is the usual and most valued picking.
appearance_dry: Plump, stout leaf in a deep green.
taste_profile: Fresh and mellow with a returning sweetness, carried by a strong aroma from the tree variety itself.

brewing.notes: General guidance for a sturdy green tea rather than a local rule: use water a little off the boil in a glass or gaiwan. The leaf is said to take repeated steeping well, so do not throw it out after the first.

vintage_note: The protected name covers a green tea, and like other Chinese greens it is normally sold as the current year's harvest and best drunk within about a year. Look for the grade (bud-level top grade or the leafier standard grade) and the geographical indication mark, which is licensed through the Nanchuan tea association.
description:
Nanchuan Dashu means big tree tea from Nanchuan, and the name is literal. It comes from a tree-form landrace that grows wild in the Jinfo Mountain area in southwest Chongqing, on karst slopes between 800 and 1600 metres. That plant is the point of the tea: most Chongqing greens come from ordinary bushes.

Only five townships fall inside the protected area: Delong, Hexi, Guhua, Dayou and the Mazui village of Sanquan. The climate is cool and very wet, with fog on around 260 days a year, and the soil is mildly acidic.

In the cup it is yellow-green and bright, fresh and mellow, with a sweetness that comes back after you swallow. Trial batches have been described as high in aroma, strong in flavour and durable over several steeps. Brew it like any sturdy green and keep the water just under boiling.

The protected product is green tea, though research trials also tried the leaf as oolong and as broken black tea and rated those results well, the oolong especially. Those are experiments rather than the established product. When buying, check for the geographical indication mark, since the appeal of big old trees makes this kind of name easy to borrow.
history:
The tree has been studied under the name Camellia nanchuanica, and local accounts put the largest specimen at more than 1400 years old, a figure best read as a local estimate. Reported amino acid levels reach 4.3%, which is high for tea.

China's Ministry of Agriculture registered Nanchuan Dashu Tea as a protected agricultural geographical indication on 3 August 2012. The registration is held by the Nanchuan district tea association. Little is documented about how the tea was drunk or traded before then.
